title: You’re Not Just Raising a Child Who Behaves. You’re Showing Them What God Is Like—or Isn’t.
paragraphs: You’re Not Just Raising a Child Who Behaves. You’re Showing Them What God Is Like—or Isn’t.

Your child may obey every rule in your house and still grow up with the wrong picture of God. Christian parenting was never meant to produce children who merely behave—it is meant to point human hearts toward the Father revealed in Jesus Christ.
There is a kind of silence in a house that can fool a parent.
The children are quiet.
Nobody is arguing.
Nobody is talking back.
The room is clean.
The rules are being followed.
And for a moment, everything looks successful.
But sometimes that silence is not peace.
Sometimes it is fear.
Sometimes the child sitting quietly at the table is not thinking, “I understand why Mom corrected me.”
He is thinking, “I better not make Dad angry.”
Sometimes the daughter who immediately says, “Yes, Mom,” is not learning wisdom.
She is learning how to avoid punishment.
Sometimes what adults celebrate as obedience is actually a frightened little heart becoming extremely skilled at reading the emotional temperature of the room.
And that should make every Christian parent uncomfortable.
Because you are not merely teaching your child how to behave around you.

Day after day, through correction, affection, patience, anger, confession, forgiveness, consistency, inconsistency, tenderness, discipline, and grace, you are helping shape their earliest understanding of authority.
And somewhere inside that experience, they are beginning to form ideas about God.
That is why one sentence from Paul should stop Christian parents in their tracks:
“Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ Κυρίου.”
Ephesians 6:4.
Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Notice what Christianity does not say.
It does not say:
Make them scared enough to obey.
Embarrass them until they change.
Control them until they become manageable.
Demand perfection so the family looks spiritual.
Win every argument.
Make sure everyone at church thinks you have wonderful children.
Paul reaches deeper.
The Greek word translated “provoke to anger” is παροργίζετε — parorgizete, carrying the idea of provoking or stirring someone toward anger.
Then comes ἐκτρέφετε — ektrephete: nourish, bring up, rear, care for.
Think about that contrast.
Do not continually provoke them.
Bring them up.
Nourish them.
And how?
“In the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
The word παιδείᾳ — paideia can refer to training, education, upbringing, or discipline. νουθεσίᾳ — nouthesia carries the sense of instruction, admonition, or corrective counsel.
This is far richer than making children behave.
Christian parenting is formative.
It reaches toward the heart.
It teaches.
Corrects.
Warns.
Models.
Nourishes.
Disciplines.
Forgives.
And continually points beyond the parent toward Christ.
That means the question after your child misbehaves cannot always be merely:
“How do I stop this behavior?”
Sometimes the more important question is:
“What does my child need to understand?”
Because behavior matters.
Scripture never teaches otherwise.

Children are called to obey their parents in the Lord. Parents are responsible to teach, correct, and discipline. Biblical grace is not parental passivity, and love is not pretending rebellion does not matter.
But outward obedience and inward discipleship are not identical.
A child can learn to say the right words while resentment grows underneath them.
A teenager can learn how to perform Christianity while secretly counting the days until leaving home.
A child can memorize Scripture and simultaneously believe that admitting failure is dangerous.
A family can look beautifully Christian in a Sunday photograph while everyone inside the house knows which subjects must never be mentioned because Dad might explode.
That is the scandal nobody wants posted on Facebook.
Sometimes our children meet our Christian reputation before they experience our Christian character.
We tell them God is patient...
then lose control when milk spills.
We tell them God forgives...
then resurrect something they did six months ago.
We tell them God welcomes confession...
then make honesty so frightening that lying feels safer.
We tell them Jesus is gentle...
then use humiliation as discipline.
We tell them their identity is found in Christ...
then act as though their grades determine their worth.
We tell them grace cannot be earned...
then withdraw affection when they disappoint us.
And children notice contradictions adults think they have successfully hidden.
This does not mean a parent must become perfect.
If perfection were required to raise children faithfully, no human being would qualify.
The Gospel begins with something far more hopeful:
You are a sinner raising sinners who desperately need the same Savior.
That changes everything.
Because one of the greatest gifts Christian parents can give their children is not the illusion of flawless parents.
It is the experience of repentant ones.
Imagine a father standing outside his child's bedroom after losing his temper.
Everything inside him wants to justify himself.
“He shouldn't have talked back.”
“I already told her three times.”
“They know better.”
“I've had a terrible day.”
Maybe every sentence contains some truth.
But none of those truths erase his sin.
So he opens the door.
He sits beside his child.
And instead of delivering another lecture, he says something that child may remember thirty years later:
“I was right to correct what you did. But the way I spoke to you was wrong. I sinned against you. Will you forgive me?”
Something enormous happens in that moment.
Authority does not disappear.
Discipline has not been abandoned.
The parent has not surrendered leadership.
The Gospel has entered the room.
The child is discovering that Christianity has somewhere to put failure.
At the cross.
This is what separates Gospel-centered parenting from image-centered parenting.
Image-centered parenting asks:
“What will people think of my child?”
Gospel-centered parenting asks:
“What is happening in my child's heart?”
Image-centered parenting is terrified of embarrassment.
Gospel-centered parenting is concerned with formation.
Image-centered parenting needs the child to make the parent look successful.
Gospel-centered parenting remembers that the child belongs ultimately to God.
And perhaps most importantly, Gospel-centered parenting allows children to watch their parents need Jesus too.
Your child should not grow up believing Christianity is a religion for people who never fail.
Let them discover that Christianity is about a Savior who came precisely because we do.
Jesus did not come for polished families with immaculate reputations.
He came for sinners.
He came for exhausted mothers.
Impatient fathers.
Angry teenagers.
Defiant children.
Broken marriages.
Wounded families.
People carrying things nobody else knows about.
People who have said things they wish they could pull back into their mouths.
People who have slammed doors.
People who have cried behind locked bathroom doors.
People who love God and still discover frightening amounts of selfishness inside themselves.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good families can become slightly better.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ bore our sins.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ offers forgiveness.
Christ gives new life.
And when that Gospel begins saturating a home, discipline changes.
Not because consequences disappear.
Because redemption becomes the destination.
The goal is no longer merely:
“You broke the rule.”
It becomes:
“Something happening in your heart produced this behavior, and I love you too much to ignore it.”
Now correction becomes an opportunity for discipleship.
Why did you lie?
Were you afraid?
Why did you hit your brother?
What were you wanting so badly that anger took control?
Why did you hide what happened?
Did you think telling me the truth would cost you my love?
Those conversations take longer than shouting.
They require patience.
They interrupt schedules.
They expose the parent's heart too.
But hearts are rarely discipled efficiently.
Children need truth repeated.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Much like adults do.
And there will be nights when you get it wrong.
You will become impatient.
You will speak before thinking.
You will discipline from irritation rather than wisdom.
You may discover patterns inherited from your own childhood coming out of your mouth.
Perhaps that is where this article becomes painful.
Because some parents reading this are suddenly remembering another house.
Another voice.
Another childhood.
Maybe you were raised where obedience was everything.
You learned early that mistakes brought humiliation.
Maybe affection disappeared when you failed.
Maybe Scripture itself was sometimes used like a weapon.
Maybe nobody apologized because adults were always right.
And now, years later, you hear yourself saying things you swore you would never say.
That realization can feel devastating.
But listen carefully.
Your family's story does not have to end where it began.
This is exactly where grace becomes more than a theological word.
Jesus Christ redeems sinners.
The cross means your worst parenting moment does not have to become the final chapter of your family.
Repentance can interrupt generations.
Grace can enter patterns that seemed permanent.
A father can learn tenderness.
A mother can learn patience.
A wounded adult can discover that biblical authority does not require cruelty.
A family can learn confession.
Children can witness restoration.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
This is our theme for a reason:
Not because consequences magically vanish.
Not because wounds never leave scars.
Not because repentance erases history.
But because Jesus can take sinners who finally stop defending themselves and begin transforming them by His grace.
Parents, your children do not need you to pretend you are Jesus.
They need you to keep pointing them to Jesus.
When you discipline them, point them toward Jesus.
When they fail, point them toward Jesus.
When they succeed, point them toward Jesus.
When you fail them, repent and point them toward Jesus.
When they ask questions you cannot answer, search Scripture with them and point them toward Jesus.
When their faith struggles, resist the temptation to panic over appearances. Listen. Pray. Speak truth. Stay present. Point them toward Jesus.
Your authority has limits.
His does not.
Your patience has limits.
His does not.
Your wisdom has limits.
His does not.
You cannot regenerate your child's heart.
You cannot manufacture saving faith.
You cannot yell someone into loving God.
You cannot control a soul into surrendering to Christ.
You can teach.
You can discipline.
You can pray.
You can model repentance.
You can confess.
You can forgive.
You can open Scripture.
You can proclaim Christ.
You can create a home where truth and grace are not enemies.
And then you entrust the heart of your child to God.
Maybe tonight your child does not need another sermon about what they did wrong.
Maybe they need a conversation.
Maybe you need to knock on a bedroom door.
Maybe there is an apology you have delayed because you thought apologizing would weaken your authority.
It won't.
Hypocrisy weakens Christian witness far more than repentance does.
Maybe the sentence your child needs tonight is:
“I love you too much to pretend what you did was okay. But nothing you did tonight makes me stop loving you. We are going to deal with this truthfully, and we are going to walk through it together.”
What a small glimpse of the Gospel that can become.
Truth without abandonment.
Correction without rejection.
Discipline surrounded by love.
Not perfect parenting.
Christian parenting.
And if reading this exposed something uncomfortable in you, do not run from it.
Bring it to Christ.
If you have wounded your children, repent before God and, where appropriate, seek their forgiveness.
If your discipline has become rage, do not rename it “biblical authority.”
If your desire for obedience has become a desire for control, confess it.
If you have cared more about how your children make you look than who they are becoming before God, confess that too.
There is mercy at the cross.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Mercy that calls sinners out of hiding and into transformation.
Maybe your children will someday forget many of the rules you made.
They may forget which chores happened on Tuesdays.
They may forget the lectures.
They may forget the consequences.
But they may remember something much deeper.
What happened when they told you the truth.
What your face looked like when they failed.
Whether correction felt like guidance or humiliation.
Whether home was a place where sin was confronted but confession was safe.
Whether Dad could say, “Forgive me.”
Whether Mom could admit, “I was wrong.”
Whether Jesus seemed like Someone the family actually needed—or merely Someone whose name appeared on decorations and Sunday schedules.
So ask yourself the difficult question:
What picture of God is my parenting helping my child imagine?
Not because you perfectly represent God. You don't.
No parent does.
But because Christian parents have been entrusted with the extraordinary responsibility of raising children “in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
That responsibility should humble us.
And send us running toward grace.
And don't keep this conversation inside your own house.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Financial support is never a substitute for obedience to Christ, but voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
Not to prove that you love God.
Not to purchase His blessing.
Not because an algorithm measures faithfulness.
But because somewhere behind another screen may be a tired mother crying after losing her temper...
a father terrified that he is becoming the man who wounded him...
a parent who thinks the damage is already too deep...
or a grown child who needs to discover that what happened in their childhood was not an accurate picture of the heart of Jesus.
Send truth into their story.
And tonight, before correcting your child's behavior again, remember what is standing in front of you.
Not an inconvenience.
Not an embarrassment.
Not a reputation-management problem.
A soul.
A human being entrusted to your care for a little while.
Teach them truth.
Give wise discipline.
Set boundaries.
Require obedience.
But let them also witness mercy.
Let them hear repentance.
Let them experience forgiveness.
Let them discover that authority does not have to mean humiliation.
And above everything else, let them see a mother or father who keeps returning to Jesus.
Because one day your child may walk out of your house carrying far more than memories of your rules.
They may carry an image of what authority, forgiveness, confession, discipline, mercy, and love feel like.
Make sure that when your parenting fails to show them the Father clearly, your repentance points them back to the Son.
Your child does not need a parent who never falls; they need to see where a Christian goes after the fall—and watch you walk back to Jesus.
